items.title: FERPA — "school official" exception letting a vendor handle education records without consent
items.applies_to_vendor: A school/LEA may disclose personally identifiable information (PII) from education records to LOVELEEDAY without parent/eligible-student consent only if LOVELEEDAY is treated as a 'school official' with a legitimate educational interest. That requires LOVELEEDAY to (1) perform an institutional service or function the school would otherwise use its own employees for, (2) be under the school's direct control regarding use and maintenance of the records, and (3) be bound by the redisclosure limits of 99.33(a) — no further disclosure without consent, use limited to the purpose disclosed.
key_obligations: Be designated a 'school official' by written agreement/contract with each school or LEA client (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B))
Accept the school's direct control over the use and maintenance of the education records disclosed
Do not redisclose PII from education records to any other party without the school's/parent's prior consent (34 CFR 99.33(a)(1))
Use the information only for the purpose for which it was disclosed (34 CFR 99.33(a)(2))
Support the school's own reasonable methods to limit access to only those records for which there is a legitimate educational interest (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(ii))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Applies to 'education records' — records directly related to a student and maintained by an educational agency/institution or a party acting for it (34 CFR 99.3). No student-breach-notice mechanism to the Dept. of Education exists under FERPA itself.
items.penalties: No direct FERPA penalty runs against the vendor. FERPA's sole federal enforcement remedy is against the educational agency/institution: the Family Policy Compliance Office (now Student Privacy Policy Office) can move to withdraw federal funding for a policy or practice of FERPA violations (20 U.S.C. 1232g(b)(1)). Vendor-facing consequences (termination, liability) come from the school's own contract.
items.uncertainty: FERPA regulations do not themselves specify the required form/content of the written designation — 'reasonable methods' and 'direct control' are undefined terms interpreted case-by-case; schools vary in how formal the contract language must be.

how_to_comply.step: Include a 'school official' designation clause in every school/LEA contract or data-privacy agreement, citing 34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B) and naming the specific institutional service performed
Contractually accept the school's direct control over use/maintenance of the records and agree not to redisclose PII without consent per 34 CFR 99.33(a)
Limit LOVELEEDAY staff access to education records to those with a legitimate need tied to the contracted service
Return or destroy education records at contract end per the school's own retention terms (FERPA sets no fixed number of days)

items.attestation: A signed data-privacy agreement/contract addendum containing the 34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B) school-official language (often satisfied by signing the SDPC National Data Privacy Agreement — see us-sdpc-ndpa)
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY stores, processes, or otherwise has access to K-12 or higher-ed student education records on behalf of a school or LEA client
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY provides infrastructure only (e.g., encrypted storage it cannot itself decrypt) with no access to identifiable student records, or the school never discloses education records to LOVELEEDAY at all
items.effort: low — the compliance mechanism is a contract clause (school-official designation + redisclosure limits), not a technical build; effort rises to medium if LOVELEEDAY must also build deletion/return-of-records workflows to match contract terms.

items.title: COPPA — school-authorized consent in place of parental consent for ed-tech vendors
items.applies_to_vendor: COPPA normally requires an 'operator' to get verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from a child under 13 (16 CFR 312.5). Where a school (or school district, or after-school program acting in loco parentis) uses an ed-tech operator for a school-authorized educational purpose, the FTC allows the school to provide consent in place of the parent, PROVIDED the operator gives the school the required notice of its data-collection/use practices and uses the data only for that school-authorized purpose — not for any commercial purpose such as marketing or advertising.
key_obligations: Provide the school with clear notice of what personal information is collected from children and how it is used, before collection (COPPA notice requirement, applied to the school in place of the parent)
Use personal information collected under school authorization only to provide the requested online educational service
Do not use the information for any commercial purpose, including marketing, advertising, or profiling unrelated to the school-requested service
Maintain reasonable security for children's personal information you collect
Provide a means for the school to review, and have deleted, the child's personal information on request
items.personal_info_definition_notes: COPPA 'personal information' under 16 CFR 312.2 includes name, address, online contact info, persistent identifiers (e.g., cookies, device IDs) usable to recognize a user over time, geolocation, photos/videos/audio with a child's image or voice.
items.penalties: FTC Act civil penalties for COPPA violations (adjusted periodically) — currently up to tens of thousands of dollars per violation, assessed per affected child/per violation in FTC enforcement actions; the FTC brings these actions, not private plaintiffs.
items.effective_or_amended: 2013 COPPA Rule amendments; FTC has an open 2024/2025 rulemaking to further codify school-authorization guidance
items.uncertainty: The school-authorized-consent doctrine (16 CFR 312.5(b)(3): consent by 'a school or school district, or an after-school program or other entity acting in loco parentis') is FTC-published guidance interpreting the Rule, not a standalone regulatory provision spelling out every vendor duty in a single section — the notice/commercial-use limits are drawn from FTC's published COPPA FAQ (ftc.gov), which is authoritative FTC guidance but not itself the codified rule text.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm the product's user base and whether it collects personal information directly from children under 13
If school-authorized consent will be relied on, give the school COPPA-required notice of data practices before any collection begins
Contractually commit to use children's data solely for the school-authorized educational purpose, with no commercial/marketing use
Build data-minimization, security, and school-initiated deletion capability into the product

items.attestation: A signed notice/agreement to the school describing the operator's data practices (satisfies the FTC's school-consent framework); often bundled into the same SDPC NDPA used for FERPA
items.triggered_when: The product collects personal information (as defined in 16 CFR 312.2) directly from a child under 13, and a school is authorizing that collection for a school-authorized educational purpose
items.not_triggered_when: The product is used only by staff/adults, only by students 13 and older, or LOVELEEDAY never collects personal information directly from the child (e.g., only aggregate or de-identified analytics)
items.effort: medium — requires giving schools COPPA notice before collection and building technical/contractual controls that block any commercial use of children's data.

items.title: Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA)
items.applies_to_vendor: PPRA obligations run against the State/local educational agency (SEA/LEA) receiving ED funds, not directly against vendors. It requires parental notice/consent (or opt-out) before students take a survey, analysis, or evaluation funded by an ED program that touches one of eight protected areas (political beliefs, mental/psychological problems, sex behavior/attitudes, illegal/self-incriminating/demeaning behavior, critical appraisals of family members, privileged relationships, religious practices, or income beyond program-eligibility purposes), and gives parents rights around marketing surveys and inspection of instructional material. Where LOVELEEDAY builds or administers a survey/assessment tool, or a product that could be used to market to or collect information from students for non-educational purposes, the LEA's PPRA duties flow into the vendor contract.
key_obligations: Do not administer, or help administer, a covered survey touching one of PPRA's eight protected areas without the LEA first providing parental notice and obtaining consent (for federally funded surveys) or an opt-out opportunity
Do not use information collected through the LEA relationship to market products/services to students or their families without parental notice and opt-out rights
Support the LEA's obligation to let parents inspect instructional materials and surveys used in ED-funded programs
Flow PPRA notice/consent controls into the product if it administers surveys on the LEA's behalf
items.penalties: No FERPA/PPRA-style penalty is spelled out for a vendor directly; ED's enforcement mechanism (via the Student Privacy Policy Office, same office that handles FERPA complaints) runs against the LEA/SEA, with withdrawal of ED funding as the ultimate remedy.
items.uncertainty: ED's published PPRA guidance does not spell out specific vendor contract-clause language the way FERPA's 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B) does; the vendor obligation is inferred from the LEA's own duty flowing down through the services contract, not a PPRA provision naming vendors directly. Did not separately verify the full text of 34 CFR Part 98 section-by-section this session (relied on studentprivacy.ed.gov's summary, an official ED source).

how_to_comply.step: Identify whether the product administers surveys/assessments that could touch PPRA's eight protected areas
Build in a flag/workflow so the LEA can issue the required parental notice and consent/opt-out before a covered survey is administered
Contractually commit not to use LEA-sourced student data for marketing without the LEA's PPRA-compliant parental notice/opt-out process

items.attestation: No federal PPRA attestation form; LEAs typically add a PPRA-compliance representation/contract clause covering surveys and marketing use, often folded into the SDPC NDPA
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's product administers or processes a survey/analysis/evaluation funded by an ED program that touches one of PPRA's eight protected areas, or the product is used to market to students/families using LEA-sourced data
items.not_triggered_when: The product does not administer surveys touching the eight protected areas and is never used for marketing purposes
items.effort: low — mainly a contractual pass-through of the LEA's own notice/consent duties; no PPRA-specific technical build unless the product itself runs covered surveys.

items.title: Student Data Privacy Consortium (SDPC) National Data Privacy Agreement (NDPA) — vendor signatory process
items.citation: SDPC National Data Privacy Agreement (NDPA), current version (v2.x), Student Data Privacy Consortium / A4L Community
items.applies_to_vendor: The NDPA is a standardized, non-governmental contract template (not a statute) that districts and state alliances use so LOVELEEDAY does not have to negotiate a bespoke data-privacy agreement with every district. LOVELEEDAY signs the NDPA (which embeds FERPA school-official language and state-specific 'Exhibit G' student-data-privacy-law riders) plus 'Exhibit E' (the General Offer of Privacy Terms), which lets any other LEA adopt the same signed terms without renegotiation.
key_obligations: Sign the NDPA (core agreement) with at least one state Alliance or district, agreeing to the built-in FERPA/student-data-privacy terms
Sign Exhibit E (General Offer of Privacy Terms) so other districts can adopt the same signed terms
List the signed agreement on the SDPC Resource Registry
Comply with any state-specific rider (Exhibit G) required by the adopting district's state student-data-privacy law
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Covers 'student data' broadly as defined in the NDPA template, generally aligned to each state's student-data-privacy statute definition, which is often broader than FERPA's 'education records.'
items.penalties: Not a government-enforced instrument; breach of the NDPA is a straightforward contract breach against the signing district(s), enforceable under normal contract law/remedies in the agreement.
items.effective_or_amended: NDPA v2 in current use (A4L Community / SDPC)
items.uncertainty: The exact application/submission mechanics for a NEW vendor's first signature (as opposed to badge management for existing signatories) were not fully detailed on the pages fetched; A4L directs new applicants to its general membership/contracting process rather than a single documented vendor-onboarding page.

how_to_comply.step: Contact a state Alliance (or the district directly) using the SDPC's standard NDPA template rather than drafting a bespoke agreement
Sign the NDPA core agreement and Exhibit E (General Offer of Privacy Terms)
Confirm the signed agreement is posted to the SDPC Resource Registry and claim the SDPC Vendor Signatory Badge

items.attestation: Signed NDPA + Exhibit E on the SDPC Resource Registry; results in the SDPC Vendor Signatory Badge buyers look for
items.triggered_when: A school district or state alliance customer requires student-data-privacy contract terms and uses (or will accept) the SDPC NDPA framework
items.not_triggered_when: The district insists on its own custom DPA instead of the NDPA, or LOVELEEDAY has no K-12 district-level customers
items.effort: low — signing a pre-negotiated template is materially faster than one-off district contract negotiation; 'no additional work requirements for vendors outside of their normal contracting processes' per SDPC's own guidance.

items.title: HIPAA Privacy, Security, and Breach Notification Rules — business associate obligations
items.citation: 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164; Privacy Rule 164.502(e)/164.504(e); Security Rule 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314; Breach Notification Rule 164.402, 164.404, 164.410
items.applies_to_vendor: A vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information (PHI) on behalf of a HIPAA covered entity (or another business associate) is itself a 'business associate' and must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with each covered-entity/BA client (45 CFR 164.504(e), 164.314(a)). As a business associate, LOVELEEDAY is directly liable under the Security Rule's administrative, physical, and technical safeguards (164.308/164.310/164.312) and must notify the covered entity of any breach of unsecured PHI without unreasonable delay, and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery (164.410(b)).
key_obligations: Sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with every covered-entity or upstream-business-associate client before receiving PHI (45 CFR 164.504(e))
Conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis of potential risks/vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI (45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A))
Implement risk management measures to reduce identified risks to a reasonable level (164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B))

Apply the Security Rule's administrative, physical, and technical safeguards (access controls, audit controls, encryption where appropriate, workforce sanctions, information system activity review) (164.308, 164.310, 164.312)

Notify the covered entity of a breach of unsecured PHI without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery, including identification of affected individuals to the extent possible (164.410(a)-(c))
Only use/disclose PHI as permitted by the BAA and report unauthorized use/disclosure to the covered entity (164.504(e)(2))
items.notice_deadline: Business associate to covered entity: "without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach" (45 CFR 164.410(b))
items.regulator_notice: The covered entity (not the business associate directly, unless the BAA delegates it) must notify HHS OCR; for breaches affecting 500+ individuals, notice to HHS is required contemporaneously with individual notice, and to prominent media outlets serving the affected jurisdiction (164.408).
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Protected health information' (PHI) = individually identifiable health information held/transmitted by a covered entity or business associate, in any form (45 CFR 160.103). 'Unsecured PHI' (the breach-notification trigger) means PHI not rendered unusable/unreadable/indecipherable via HHS-specified encryption/destruction methods.
items.penalties: HHS OCR civil monetary penalties under the HITECH Act tiered structure (per-violation amounts that adjust annually for inflation, ranging from roughly hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars per violation depending on culpability tier, with an annual cap per identical violation type); willful neglect can also trigger DOJ criminal referral.
items.effective_or_amended: HIPAA Security Rule most recently proposed for major update in 2025 (NPRM); Breach Notification Rule from 2009 (HITECH), largely unchanged since 2013 Omnibus Rule.
items.uncertainty: HHS.gov's own BAA/Security Rule guidance pages returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches this session; the regulatory text itself was fetched and verified directly from ecfr.gov instead, which is the authoritative source. Exact current civil-penalty dollar tiers were not independently re-verified this session (HHS 403'd); do not quote a specific number without a fresh HHS/Federal Register check.

how_to_comply.step: Sign a Business Associate Agreement with each covered-entity (or upstream business associate) client before touching PHI
Conduct and document a HIPAA Security Rule risk analysis covering all systems that create/receive/maintain/transmit ePHI
Implement the Security Rule's required/addressable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards and document a remediation plan for gaps
Build and rehearse a breach-detection and 60-day covered-entity notification workflow
Flow BAA-equivalent terms down to any subcontractor (e.g., cloud host) that will also touch PHI (164.308(b)(1))

items.attestation: Signed BAA; a documented risk analysis; buyers increasingly also ask for a SOC 2 Type II report or HITRUST certification as evidence, though neither is a HIPAA legal requirement
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of a HIPAA covered entity or another business associate client
items.not_triggered_when: The client is not a HIPAA covered entity/business associate, or LOVELEEDAY never receives health information (e.g., pure billing/scheduling metadata with no health content)
items.effort: high — a signed BAA per client, a documented risk analysis, a real administrative/physical/technical-safeguards program, and a rehearsed 60-day breach-notification process; this is the heaviest-effort item in this set.

items.title: 42 CFR Part 2 — Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records; Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA)
items.citation: 42 U.S.C. 290dd-2; 42 CFR Part 2, definitions at 42 CFR 2.11
items.applies_to_vendor: Part 2 governs records of federally assisted substance use disorder (SUD) treatment programs — a stricter confidentiality regime than HIPAA. A vendor providing services (e.g., data processing) to a Part 2 program is a 'qualified service organization' (QSO) only if it has a written Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA) with the Part 2 program under which it (1) acknowledges it is fully bound by Part 2's regulations in receiving/storing/processing patient records, and (2) will, if necessary, resist in judicial proceedings any effort to obtain unauthorized access to patient-identifying information, disclosing only that a court order exists (42 CFR 2.11).
key_obligations: Sign a written Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA) with each Part 2 program client (42 CFR 2.11)
Acknowledge in the QSOA that LOVELEEDAY is fully bound by 42 CFR Part 2 when receiving, storing, processing, or otherwise dealing with patient records
Agree to resist, in judicial proceedings, efforts to obtain access to patient-identifying SUD information beyond what the regulations/QSOA permit
Do not redisclose SUD patient-identifying information except as permitted by Part 2 (general rule: no redisclosure without specific written patient consent or a qualifying exception)
items.regulator_notice: Complaints of noncompliance may be filed with HHS in the same manner as HIPAA complaints (42 CFR 2.4(b), referencing 45 CFR 160.306) following 2024 rule changes that aligned Part 2 enforcement with HIPAA.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Protects 'records' of any individual who has applied for or received SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral for treatment from a federally assisted Part 2 program — broader confidentiality than general HIPAA PHI in that even the existence of treatment is protected.
items.penalties: Criminal fines for disclosure violations under 42 U.S.C. 290dd-2; since the 2024 rule alignment, HHS OCR also applies HIPAA's civil-penalty enforcement structure to Part 2 breach-notification and enforcement provisions.
items.effective_or_amended: 2024 final rule (89 FR 12472, Feb. 16, 2024) substantially aligned Part 2 with HIPAA
items.uncertainty: Did not locate/verify the specific section number establishing the QSOA as a disclosure exception (distinct from the §2.11 QSO definition itself) within this session's page fetch; the definitional text at §2.11 is confirmed, but the operative permitting-disclosure section should be re-confirmed before drafting an actual QSOA.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm whether the health-industry client is a federally assisted SUD ('Part 2') program as opposed to a general health provider
Sign a Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA) with the Part 2 program before receiving any SUD patient records
Layer Part 2's stricter redisclosure limits on top of the existing HIPAA BAA safeguards program (see us-hipaa-business-associate-obligations)

items.triggered_when: The health-sector client is a federally assisted substance use disorder program and LOVELEEDAY receives, stores, or processes SUD patient-identifying records
items.not_triggered_when: The client is a general health provider with no federally assisted SUD program, or LOVELEEDAY never touches SUD-specific patient records
items.effort: medium — mainly a signed QSOA; the underlying technical safeguards largely overlap with the HIPAA Security Rule program already required for any health client.

items.title: FTC Health Breach Notification Rule — third-party service provider notice duty
items.applies_to_vendor: This Rule applies to vendors of personal health records (PHR), PHR-related entities, and their third-party service providers that are NOT HIPAA covered entities or business associates (it does not apply where HIPAA already covers the activity). As a third-party service provider, LOVELEEDAY must, following discovery of a breach of security, notify an official designated in a written contract by the PHR vendor/PHR-related entity client (or, absent a designation, a senior official) and obtain acknowledgment of receipt; the notice must identify each customer whose unsecured PHR identifiable health information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired.
key_obligations: Determine, in the contract with each PHR vendor/PHR-related-entity client, who the designated official for breach notices is (16 CFR 318.3(b))
Following discovery of a security breach, notify that designated official and obtain acknowledgment that notice was received
Include in the notice the identification of each customer whose unsecured PHR identifiable health information has been, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired
Be notified BY the client of its status as a vendor of personal health records/PHR-related entity subject to this Part, so LOVELEEDAY knows the Rule applies (318.3(b))
items.notice_deadline: No fixed number of days is stated for the third-party-service-provider-to-client notice itself; the Rule's timeliness clock (as soon as possible and, per §318.4, without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days) runs against the vendor of personal health records/PHR-related entity for notices to individuals, the FTC, and media.
items.regulator_notice: The vendor of personal health records/PHR-related entity (the service provider's client, not LOVELEEDAY itself in most cases) must notify the FTC, and media outlets if 500+ residents of a state/jurisdiction are affected (16 CFR 318.3(a)(2)-(3)).
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'PHR identifiable health information' = individually identifiable health information in a personal health record, as defined by reference to HIPAA's 'individually identifiable health information' standard, held outside the HIPAA-covered ecosystem.
items.penalties: FTC Act Section 5 civil penalties for violations, assessed by the FTC; this Rule was substantially amended and its enforcement posture strengthened in 2024 (89 FR 47054, May 30, 2024).
items.uncertainty: None material — full operative text of 318.3(b) was fetched and quoted directly from ecfr.gov this session.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm with each health-adjacent client whether it is a 'vendor of personal health records' or 'PHR related entity' under this Rule (as opposed to a HIPAA covered entity/business associate, where the HIPAA rule applies instead)
Add a contract clause naming the designated official to receive LOVELEEDAY's breach notices, per 16 CFR 318.3(b)
Build a breach-detection and prompt-notification workflow that identifies affected customers and obtains acknowledgment of receipt from the designated official

items.attestation: Written contract naming the designated recipient of third-party-service-provider breach notices under 16 CFR 318.3(b)
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is a third-party service provider to a vendor of personal health records or PHR-related entity that is not a HIPAA covered entity/business associate for that data
items.not_triggered_when: The client is a HIPAA covered entity, or LOVELEEDAY is itself a HIPAA business associate for that data set (then the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule applies instead — see us-hipaa-business-associate-obligations)
items.effort: low — the vendor-facing duty is a contract clause plus a straightforward notify-and-get-acknowledgment workflow; the heavier consumer/FTC/media notice burden sits with the PHR vendor/PHR-related-entity client, not LOVELEEDAY.

items.title: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) — FTC Safeguards Rule, service-provider oversight
items.applies_to_vendor: GLBA's 'financial institution' definition is broad — it reaches many businesses beyond banks that are 'significantly engaged' in financial activities (lending, loan servicing, investment advice, etc.), and the FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) applies to those institutions directly. LOVELEEDAY, as a service provider to such a client, is not itself directly regulated by Part 314, but the client is REQUIRED to (a) retain responsibility for compliance even if it uses a service provider's staff to fill the 'Qualified Individual' role, and (b) select and retain service providers 'capable of maintaining appropriate safeguards,' REQUIRE THEM BY CONTRACT to implement and maintain those safeguards, and periodically assess them (16 CFR 314.4(f)). In practice this means LOVELEEDAY must contractually commit to, and actually run, an information-security program meeting Part 314's substance.
key_obligations: Expect and accept a contract clause requiring LOVELEEDAY to implement/maintain safeguards equivalent to the client's own Part 314 program (16 CFR 314.4(f)(2))
Support a written, periodically updated risk assessment covering the customer information LOVELEEDAY handles (314.4(b))

Implement access controls, encryption of customer information in transit and at rest (or documented compensating controls), secure development practices, and multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing information systems (314.4(c))
Maintain a written incident response plan (314.4(h))
Cooperate with the client's periodic risk-based assessment of LOVELEEDAY as a service provider (314.4(f)(3))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Customer information' = nonpublic personal information about a customer of a financial institution, whether handled by the institution or by a service provider on its behalf (16 CFR 314.2(d)).
items.penalties: FTC Act Section 5 enforcement; civil penalties for Safeguards Rule violations can reach tens of thousands of dollars per violation (inflation-adjusted), plus potential consent-decree obligations; a service provider that caused the underlying failure can face its own FTC scrutiny where it independently engaged in unfair/deceptive practices.
items.effective_or_amended: Major amendments effective 2021-2023 (2021 rule; general compliance deadline June 9, 2023) adding the Qualified Individual, MFA, encryption, and service-provider-oversight requirements
items.uncertainty: None material — full operative text of 314.4 was fetched and quoted directly from ecfr.gov this session.

how_to_comply.step: Identify which clients qualify as 'financial institutions' under GLBA's broad activity-based definition (not just banks)
Accept and be ready to sign the client's Safeguards Rule service-provider contract clause (314.4(f)(2))
Build/document a written risk assessment, access controls, encryption, MFA, secure-development practices, and an incident response plan matching 314.4(b)-(h)
Cooperate with the client's periodic reassessment of LOVELEEDAY as a service provider

items.attestation: Contract clause requiring safeguards (16 CFR 314.4(f)(2)); financial-institution customers increasingly ask for a SOC 2 Type II report or a completed security questionnaire as evidence
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is a service provider handling 'customer information' (nonpublic personal financial information) on behalf of a client that qualifies as a 'financial institution' under GLBA's broad definition
items.not_triggered_when: The client is not a GLBA 'financial institution,' or LOVELEEDAY's role never touches customer financial data
items.effort: high — the client will contractually require a real written information-security program (risk assessment, access controls, encryption, MFA, incident response); this is engineering and policy work, not just paperwork.

items.title: SEC Regulation S-P (2024 amendments) — service-provider breach notification for broker-dealers and investment advisers
items.applies_to_vendor: The 2024 Reg S-P amendments require 'covered institutions' (SEC-registered broker-dealers, investment companies, and registered investment advisers) to have written policies and procedures requiring oversight — including due diligence and monitoring — of their service providers, designed to ensure those service providers (1) protect against unauthorized access to customer information and (2) notify the covered institution 'as soon as possible, but no later than 72 hours' after becoming aware of a breach affecting a customer information system the service provider maintains (17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)(i)). LOVELEEDAY, as such a service provider, will be contractually bound to that 72-hour notice clock, which then triggers the covered institution's own investor-notification process (generally within 30 days).
key_obligations: Accept a written service-provider oversight agreement from each broker-dealer/investment-adviser client (17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)(i))
Protect against unauthorized access to or use of customer information (248.30(a)(5)(i)(A))

Notify the covered institution as soon as possible, but no later than 72 hours, after becoming aware of a security breach resulting in unauthorized access to a customer information system LOVELEEDAY maintains (248.30(a)(5)(i)(B))

Optionally, by separate written agreement, handle affected-individual notification on the covered institution's behalf — but legal responsibility for that notice always remains with the covered institution (248.30(a)(5)(ii)-(iii))
items.notice_deadline: Service provider to covered institution: "as soon as possible, but no later than 72 hours" after becoming aware of the breach (17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)(i)(B)). Covered institution to affected individuals: "as soon as practicable, but not later than 30 days" after becoming aware (17 CFR 248.30(a)(4)(iii)).
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Customer information' / 'sensitive customer information' under Reg S-P covers nonpublic personal information a covered institution or its service provider handles about the institution's customers, including data that could be used to commit identity theft.
items.penalties: SEC enforcement action for violating Reg S-P's safeguards/notification requirements; penalties are case-by-case (cease-and-desist orders, civil monetary penalties) under SEC enforcement authority.
items.effective_or_amended: Amendments adopted May 2024 (Release No. 34-100155); large entities compliance date December 2025, smaller entities June 2026
items.uncertainty: None material — full operative text of 248.30(a)(4)-(5) was fetched and quoted directly from ecfr.gov this session. Compliance-date phase-in (Dec 2025 for larger entities / June 2026 for smaller) was reported by the rule's adopting release and not independently re-verified against a live SEC.gov page this session.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm whether the client is an SEC 'covered institution' (registered broker-dealer, investment company, or registered investment adviser) subject to Reg S-P
Sign the client's service-provider oversight/due-diligence agreement including the 72-hour breach-notice clause
Build a breach-detection and 72-hour notification workflow to the covered institution
Decide, per client, whether LOVELEEDAY will also handle investor notification on the covered institution's behalf via a separate written agreement

items.attestation: Written service-provider agreement establishing the 72-hour breach-notification duty under 17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is a service provider to an SEC-registered broker-dealer, investment company, or registered investment adviser and maintains a customer information system for that client
items.not_triggered_when: The client is not SEC-registered (e.g., a private real-estate portfolio company with no broker-dealer/RIA registration — GLBA/Safeguards Rule may still apply instead; see us-glba-ftc-safeguards-rule)
items.effort: medium-high — requires a written 72-hour breach-notice agreement and an incident-response workflow fast enough to actually hit that window.

items.title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 — Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) scope and hosted/tokenized payment page reduction
items.citation: PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) v4.0.1, PCI Security Standards Council; SAQ A, SAQ A-EP, SAQ D (Merchant and Service Provider)
items.applies_to_vendor: PCI DSS applies to any entity that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, or that could impact the security of the cardholder data environment (CDE) — including a software vendor whose code runs on a client's payment page. If LOVELEEDAY's software ever touches cardholder data directly, LOVELEEDAY itself becomes a PCI DSS 'service provider' subject to the full SAQ D-SP / QSA-assessed requirements. If LOVELEEDAY instead architects payments through a fully hosted or tokenized third-party checkout (e.g., a redirect or an iframe/drop-in widget where no LOVELEEDAY-served code touches card fields), both LOVELEEDAY and the hospitality/retail/nonprofit client stay eligible for the lightest self-assessment, SAQ A (only ~24 requirements), and LOVELEEDAY can often stay entirely out of PCI scope.
key_obligations: Determine whether any LOVELEEDAY-built or LOVELEEDAY-hosted code touches cardholder data or the payment page at all

If touching card data: implement the full PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement set and complete the applicable SAQ (or full Report on Compliance if a large service provider) with an Attestation of Compliance (AOC)

If NOT touching card data: confirm and document the eligibility criteria for SAQ A — payment fully outsourced to a PCI DSS compliant third-party service provider (TPSP), no electronic storage/processing/transmission of account data on LOVELEEDAY or client systems, and (for e-commerce) every element of the payment page originates directly from the compliant TPSP
Review the TPSP's own PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance annually
Reassess PCI scope whenever the payment integration architecture changes (e.g., adding any client-side script that touches the card fields moves the merchant from SAQ A to SAQ A-EP or higher)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Account data' = cardholder data (PAN, cardholder name, expiration date, service code) plus sensitive authentication data (full track data, CVV, PINs/PIN blocks); PCI DSS is a payment-brand contractual standard, not a government regulation, so there is no 'personal info' statutory definition — scope is defined by the PCI SSC's own Applicability Information.
items.penalties: Not government-imposed; enforcement runs through the card networks/acquiring banks via merchant/processor agreements — fines, increased transaction fees, or loss of card-acceptance privileges for non-compliance or after a breach involving unsecured cardholder data.
items.effective_or_amended: PCI DSS v4.0.1 (June 2024); SAQs for v4.0.1 published October 2024; PCI DSS v4.0 retired December 31, 2024
items.uncertainty: The precise SAQ A eligibility bullet list quoted was fetched from the PCI SSC's published SAQ A document (April 2022, aligned to PCI DSS v4.0); the PCI SSC's own October 2024 bulletin confirms v4.0.1 SAQs 'clarified' (not overhauled) the SAQ A/A-EP eligibility criteria, but the exact v4.0.1-dated SAQ A PDF text was not independently re-fetched this session — verify against the current-dated SAQ A document before finalizing a client's specific SAQ determination.

how_to_comply.step: Map the payment integration architecture and confirm no LOVELEEDAY-served code touches cardholder data (use a hosted redirect or tokenized iframe/drop-in widget from a PCI DSS compliant processor)
If eligible, have the client complete SAQ A (fully outsourced, card-not-present) with its Attestation of Compliance

If any LOVELEEDAY script/redirect mechanism sits on infrastructure LOVELEEDAY or the client controls, plan for SAQ A-EP instead and implement the additional network/application security controls it requires
Collect and review the payment processor/TPSP's PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance annually

items.attestation: Attestation of Compliance (AOC) for the applicable SAQ (A, A-EP, or D/D-SP for a service provider that touches card data); for a fully tokenized/hosted integration, reliance on the payment processor's own AOC is the norm
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's software stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data for a hospitality/retail/nonprofit-donation client, or any LOVELEEDAY-served script/redirect mechanism is part of the payment page
items.not_triggered_when: Payments run entirely through a hosted/redirect checkout or a tokenized drop-in widget (e.g., a compliant processor's hosted page or iframe) with no LOVELEEDAY-served code touching the card fields — this keeps both LOVELEEDAY and the client eligible for SAQ A and typically keeps LOVELEEDAY fully out of PCI DSS scope
items.effort: low if fully tokenized/hosted (an architecture choice made once, not ongoing compliance work); high if LOVELEEDAY's systems ever touch raw cardholder data (full SAQ D-SP or QSA assessment, recurring annually).

items.title: 2 CFR Part 200 (Uniform Guidance) — obligations that flow down to contractors of federally funded grantees
items.applies_to_vendor: Uniform Guidance governs how a nonprofit or local-government 'recipient'/'subrecipient' of federal grant funds spends that money, including on vendors. Under 200.331, LOVELEEDAY is almost always a 'contractor' (procuring goods/services within LOVELEEDAY's normal business operations, offered to many customers, not subject to the federal program's own compliance requirements) rather than a 'subrecipient' (which carries the recipient's own full compliance burden, including single-audit exposure). As a contractor, LOVELEEDAY is not directly regulated by Uniform Guidance, but the client (as recipient/subrecipient) must (a) maintain procurement oversight to ensure LOVELEEDAY performs per contract terms (200.318(b)), and (b) give the federal awarding agency, Inspectors General, the Comptroller General, or a pass-through entity 'timely and reasonable' access to LOVELEEDAY's records pertinent to the federal award, and to LOVELEEDAY's personnel for interviews about them (200.337(a)) — a right that lasts as long as the records are retained, not just for the standard retention period.
key_obligations: Accept the client's contractual right of oversight to ensure LOVELEEDAY performs per the terms, conditions, and specifications of the contract (200.318(b))

Provide the federal awarding agency, Inspectors General, Comptroller General, pass-through entity, or their authorized representatives timely and reasonable access to LOVELEEDAY records pertinent to the federal award, and to relevant personnel for interview, for as long as those records are retained (200.337(a))

Support the client's records-retention schedule (generally three years from submission of the final expenditure report, longer in specified circumstances) for anything pertinent to the award (200.334)

Accept any federally required flow-down contract clauses the client must include (e.g., equal-opportunity, debarment, whistleblower-protection clauses from 2 CFR Part 200 Appendix II) even though LOVELEEDAY itself is a contractor, not a subrecipient
items.penalties: No direct federal penalty runs against a contractor under Uniform Guidance; enforcement runs against the recipient/subrecipient (the client), which can face disallowed costs, funding conditions, suspension, or debarment for procurement or oversight failures — consequences that flow back into the vendor relationship contractually, not through direct federal action against LOVELEEDAY.
items.effective_or_amended: 89 FR 30136, April 22, 2024 (most recent Uniform Guidance revision)
items.uncertainty: The exact list of Appendix II flow-down clauses potentially applicable to a given LOVELEEDAY contract was not independently pulled this session; the general oversight/records-access/retention framework (200.318, 200.331, 200.334, 200.337) is directly sourced and confirmed.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm with the nonprofit/local-government client whether the specific engagement is paid from a federal award, and whether LOVELEEDAY is being treated as a contractor (normal case) or a subrecipient
Accept a records-access clause giving the federal agency/pass-through entity/Inspectors General/Comptroller General timely access to records pertinent to the award, for as long as they're retained
Match LOVELEEDAY's own records-retention practice to the client's federal retention schedule for anything pertinent to the award (generally 3 years from final expenditure report)
Review and accept any Appendix II flow-down clauses the client's grant terms require in the vendor contract

items.attestation: No federal attestation form for a 'contractor' (as distinct from a 'subrecipient'); the procurement contract/purchase order itself, plus any required Appendix II flow-down clauses, is the instrument
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is under contract to a nonprofit or local-government client that is a recipient or subrecipient of federal grant funds, and LOVELEEDAY's services are paid for in whole or part from that federal award
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is paid from the client's unrestricted/non-federal funds, or the relationship is structured (correctly, per 200.331(b)) as a standard commercial contractor arrangement rather than a subrecipient relationship
items.effort: low for a normal contractor relationship (records-access clause + retention alignment); would become high only if LOVELEEDAY were misclassified as a 'subrecipient,' which pulls in full Uniform Guidance subpart F single-audit exposure — worth confirming contractor status explicitly in each grant-funded contract.
